# Executive summary 

The differences in the pace of recovery amongst the world’s major economies is becoming more pronounced.  China, the pace setter for the developing world, continues to lead.  The US and Japanese economies have followed strongly while the European economies are starting to stumble and are in danger of being left behind.  While this divergence is somewhat extreme at the moment, copper consumption over the next 15 years is forecast to follow a similar divergent path.  The urbanisation and industrialisation of the developing world will fuel strong demand growth for copper.  In stark contrast, demand for copper in the world’s mature economies is in long-term decline.  Demand from the mature economies during the forecast period 2010-2025 is expected to decline by 2.3% p.a., down from 5.4Mt in 2009 to 3.7Mt by 2025.  In contrast, demand from the developing economies is estimated to increase by 4.9% p.a. during the forecast period, up from 11.8Mt in 2009 to 25.5Mt by 2025.  Global refined copper consumption, overall, is forecast to increase by 3.4% p.a. through to 2025, where demand will rise from 17.2Mt in 2009 to ~29.3Mt in 2025. 

We now expect base case mine production _capability_ to increase by 1.9% during 2010, to ~16.4Mt, by 6.1% in 2011, to ~17.3Mt, and by 5.4% in 2012 to ~18.3Mt.  In 2013 mine production capability is expected to be relatively unchanged at ~18.3Mt.  However, based on current plans, the general trend in base case mine production capability is for a steady decline from 2014 onwards as output is lost, either to mine closures, or grade attrition exceeding committed incremental expansion or committed new base case project capacity.  During the forecast period the greatest loss in mine production capability will occur in Latin America, followed by North America, Oceania, Asia, Europe and Africa.  China is the only region where mine production capability is expected to increase during the forecast period. 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1.5% p.a. between 2010 (inclusive) and 2025 with output falling from a peak of ~18.3Mt in 2013 to ~12.6Mt in 2025.  However, note that this rate of decline excludes our mine disruption allowance (5% of initial mine production capability forecast) and any price related/market adjustment.  At the same time, demand for additional mine production (including the disruption allowance) to meet increased market requirements for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine output of ~0.4Mt/a in 2011, ~0.7Mt/a in 2013, 7Mt/a in 2020 and ~13.5Mt/a by 2025. 

We now expect

base case global copper smelter production capability to increase by 6.4% this year, to 15.1Mt, relative to production in 2009 and by 10.5% and 8.5% in 2011 and 2012 to 16.7Mt and 18.1Mt respectively.  The largest rise in 2010 will be seen in China with the commissioning of Baoding (200kt/a) and Liangshan (100kt/a) smelters plus several smelter expansions. 

Base case global copper refined production capability is now expected to reach 19.8Mt/a in 2010 (+7.6%), 22Mt/a in 2011 (+11.6%) and 23.7Mt/a in 2012 (+7.6%).  However, growth is forecast to slow markedly from 2014 onwards with refined production capability expected to decline from 2017 onwards.  As a consequence overall global capability will increase by only 1.5% p.a. between 2010 (inclusive) and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.9Mt to 23.2Mt in 2025. 

Demand, outside of China, has recovered at a much quicker pace than most (ourselves included) had originally anticipated during H1 this year.  However, wire rod and brass mills manufacturers alike reported that the strong order levels reflected restocking rather than any significant pick up in end-use demand.  Thus, while order levels through Q2 are reported to be strong there is concern that this momentum may not be maintained from Q3 onwards.  This was reiterated by Chinese consumers reporting that their order books in May were not be as strong as those witnessed during the first four months of the year.  This is reflected in our demand forecast of 6.1% growth in global refined copper consumption this year to just under 18.3Mt.  Previously we were forecasting an annual gain of 5.4% to just over 18.2Mt. At the same time supply growth during H1 has been restricted.  Thus we now expect global refined copper production to increase by 0.5% this year to ~18.4Mt.  This compares with our previous forecast of 1.2% growth to just under 18.6Mt. As a consequence of these revisions we have halved our global market surplus this year from ~325 t to ~150kt since our last Long Term Outlook Report.  Prices are forecast to average $6725/t ($3.05/lb) this year, up 30% from last year’s average of $5170/t ($2.34/lb).

# Demand analysis 

## Overview 

**China leads global economic recovery** The differences in the pace of recovery amongst the world’s major economies is becoming more pronounced.  China, the pace setter for the developing world, continues to lead.  The US and Japanese economies have followed strongly while the European economies are starting to stumble and are in danger of being left behind.  While this divergence is somewhat extreme at the moment, copper consumption over the next 15 years is forecast to follow a similar divergent path.  The urbanisation and industrialisation of the developing world will fuel strong demand growth for copper.  In stark contrast, demand for copper in the world’s mature economies is in long-ter

m decline.  Additional downward pressure on copper consumption in the near to medium-term will come from the need of many of the world’s mature economy governments to implement stringent austerity measures that will result in falling public sector spending, higher taxes and, as a consequence, slower economic growth.  Demand from the mature economies will also be hampered by the displacement of first-use demand away from mature economies to the developing economies where production costs will be much cheaper.  Reflecting this, demand from the mature economies during the forecast period 2010-2025 is expected to decline by 2.3% p.a., down from 5.4Mt in 2009 to 3.7Mt by 2025.  In contrast, demand from the developing economies is estimated to increase by 4.9% p.a. during the forecast period, up from 11.8Mt in 2009 to 25.5Mt by 2025.  Global refined copper consumption, overall, is forecast to increase by 3.4% p.a. through to 2025, where demand will rise from 17.2Mt in 2009 to ~29.3Mt in 2025. 

**Moderate recovery in mature economy copper demand forecast this year** As we have noted previously 2010 will be a transitional year with demand increasing more strongly in 2011.  Historically, strong sustainable first use copper demand growth has occurred 18 months to two years after the low-point in a recession-driven downturn in consumption. This is because many applications for copper in, for example, the construction sector, tend to be required towards the end of construction projects (plumbing, wiring, decorative items).  Reflecting this, demand in the mature economies is forecast to recover by 3.3% this year, to just under 5.6Mt, before increasing by a more robust 5% in 2011 to ~5.9Mt. Thereafter, demand is expected to decline on an annual basis throughout the forecast period to 2025.  As we noted in our previous Long Term Outlook report the negative trend reflects the displacement of first-use demand away from the mature economies to the developing economies, especially in China, Mexico, and Vietnam.  In recent years there has been a growing trend of copper semis manufacturers moving their production facilities to areas where production costs (labour, environmental, power etc) are considerably lower.  Prime examples include Mexico and Vietnam where two of China’s largest copper tube producers have set up new copper tube mills: Golden Dragon in Mexico and Hailiang in Vietnam.  In addition, increased exports of competitively priced copper products from China, and other developing economies into the mature economies will impact negatively on the production of copper semi products (from the mature economies), resulting in some production facilities becoming obsolete.

**Robust growth forecast in copper demand in the developing economies** Demand within the developing economies is forecast to grow by 7.4% this year, to ~12.7Mt, followed by further growth of 7.6% and 5.2% in 2011 and 2012 to 13.7Mt and 14.4Mt respectively.  The strong growth rates largely reflect robust Chinese demand which is expected to increase by 10% this year, 8% in 2011 and 5% in 2012 to ~7.2Mt, ~7.8Mt and 8.1Mt respectively.  Further out, demand will continue to improve on an annual basis where refined copper consumption within the developing economies is forecast to increase by 4.9% p.a. between 2010 (inclusive) and 2025.  Thus refined copper consumption will rise from ~11.8Mt at the end of 2009 to 25.5Mt by 2025.  Strong growth in emerging economies will be supported by continued investment within the power sector.

## China 

**China appears to be managing a controlled slowdown** The Chinese authorities are enjoying some success in managing a controlled slowdown of their over-heating economy.  The various measures that they have introduced over the past few months to reduce the availability of credit, and tame the real estate sector, have resulted in fixed asset investment slowing to more normal levels.  The tightening of credit has also impacted upon manufacturing activity where the Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) for the sector showed that the pace of expansion has slowed markedly in recent months. 

**China’s output of white goods surge** Despite the slower pace of economic growth Chinese demand for white goods remains firm, helped by the government’s subsidy scheme for home appliances.  In February last year the Chinese government launched the subsidy programme to spur consumption of home appliances, particularly in rural areas, which, in turn, helped buoy economic growth amid the global economic downturn.  The success of the programme was highlighted by the Ministry of Commerce who reported a 510% surge in the domestic sales of home appliances during the first four months of this year from the corresponding period in 2010.  In April alone, 4.8M sets of subsidised home appliances were sold, according to the government department.  This represented an annual increase of 170%.  The scheme covers home appliances such as refrigerators, television sets, washing machines, air conditioner units, mobile phones, water heaters, mi

cro-wave ovens and normal ovens. Reflecting the surge in home appliance sales the National Bureau of Statistics reported that the output of washing machines, refrigerators, freezers and air conditioner units increased annually by 34.3%, 29.7%, 48.9% and 27.5% respectively during the first four months of the year. Such strong output growth helped support demand for copper and copper alloys which increased by ~22% year on year during the same 4-month period, according to China’s Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNIA). Also positive was the recent news that the Chinese government has decided to extend the home appliance subsidy scheme. Initially the scheme was due to finish at the end of May but it has now been extended until the end of this year. ###### **Chinese production of copper and copper alloy products - (kt)** 50 % change Production 3000

**Chinese demand weakened slightly** During the quarter there has been a slight easing in demand since April where fabricators have reported slightly weaker order books, although levels are still around normal levels. Further forward, some fabricators believe that the low season might come early while exports of copper tube are expected to decline following the recent introduction of the anti dumping duty in the US. In the wire rod market production slowed recently, reflecting weaker orders for power cable in May, high inventories of copper wire rod and lower cathode off-take because of copper’s falling price. However, whilst orders for power cable may have slowed demand for magnet wire remained strong. Also, any weakness will be offset by increased demand resulting from the extension of the home appliance subsidy scheme. Thus, we have raised our 2010 Chinese demand estimate since our last report and now forecast growth of 10% where Chinese refined copper consumption will rise from 6.5Mt in 2009 to ~7.2Mt this year. **Healthy growth in Chinese copper demand during the forecast period** In 2011 we forecast that the dissipation of the impact of the government’s stimulus packages and last year’s surge in lending will be more than offset by strong demand for Chinese exports which will lift Chinese copper consumption by a further 8% to ~7.7Mt. Throughout the forecast period Chinese refined copper consumption is forecast to grow by 5.6% p.a., rising from ~6.5Mt at the end of 2009 to ~15.5Mt by 2025. The ~9Mt gain in refined consumption during this period will result in China’s share of global refined copper consumption increasing from 38% at the end of last year to a significant 53% by 2025. ## North America 

**US manufacturing activity remains in expansion territory** US manufacturing activity remained firmly in expansionary territory during the quarter.  The latest purchasing manager’s index reached 59.7 in April.  While this was down slightly from April’s reading of 60.4, the component indices remained very encouraging.  Both the output and new orders indices were unchanged at 66.9 and 65.7 respectively.  Meanwhile, the difference between new orders and inventories, a good indicator of future output, increased.  Manufacturing activity during Q2 has been much stronger than expected. 

**Improvement in wire rod demand** Reflecting the increase in manufacturing activity, some wire rod producers in the US reported a small pick up in orders during the quarter.  While it is typical for demand to be stronger at this time of year, because of the better weather leading to increased construction activity, producers have been surprised by the strength of the recovery.  According to our sources some sectors are performing better than others.  The market for magnet wire is doing reasonably well as are orders for wire and cable consumed within the renewable energy sector i.e. solar energy and wind production.  Elsewhere, the telecoms market is stronger than expected while demand for building wire remains dampened.  This is not surprising in light of the parlous state of the US construction sector. 

**Construction sector still struggling** The construction sector has yet to show any significant signs of recovery from the implosion of the housing market bubble.  The ending of the homebuyer tax credit in April has had a dramatic impact on residential construction activity.  Housing starts in May posted a 10% month on month decline to a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 593k units, the lowest rate seen this year.  However, on a slightly positive note housing starts were up 7.4% year on year in May.  Thus it is now possible that 2010 will be the first year since 2005 in which the residential construction sector will make a positive contribution to the US economy.  Nevertheless, despite this it is likely to be at least another two years before construction activity returns to more normal levels. 

**Restocking partly responsible for the stronger than expected recovery** One wire rod producer we spoke to believed that the stronger than expected rise in orders reflected restocking rather than any significant recovery in demand from the end-use markets.  Inventories throughout the supply chain were drawn down to a minimum last year and consumers of copper wire rod are now con

cerned that should there be a sudden recovery in demand for their end use products, against an improving economic outlook, they will not be able to respond sufficiently. ###### **US copper wire rod production - (kt)** 30 550

Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - June 2010 Page 7 of 46 Copper Long-term Outlook **Improving demand from the auto sector** The improvement in demand for magnet wire and, in turn wire rod, partly reflected stronger orders from the auto sector. Although vehicle production declined in April from March’s high volumes, output was still up on the prior four months. Total output in April, at 630.7k units, was up 41.3% from a year earlier. Due to dealer incentives resulting in steady increases in vehicle demand, coupled with an improving economic outlook, vehicle production is expected to be robust in the coming months. This was underlined further by GM and Ford recently reporting that they were planning to increase production, according to our sources in the US. Both companies reported positive results for Q1 and feel confident about increasing production on the back of that. It is understood that domestic US auto producers have increased market share following the recent quality problems at Toyota. **Wire rod mills still running below par** Whilst the planned increase in auto production is encouraging, wire rod producers are reported to still be operating between 50-70% of capacity. The reduced capacity rates were reflected in the latest data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics which showed that the tonnage of cathode consumed by domestic wire rod producers during Q1, while up 6.4% from a year earlier, remained significantly below levels reached in 2008. According to the ABMS cathode consumed by wire rod producers in Q1 equalled 312kt. This was up from the 293kt consumed in Q1 2009 but ~100kt below that consumed during the first quarter in 2008. **Brass mills report positive order levels during Q2** Brass mills have reported firm order levels during this quarter with some copper semi producers reporting sales above budget. They also confirmed that their customers further downstream are also reporting healthy order levels. According to our sources the positive demand reflected a combination of restocking and the possible introduction of an anti dumping duty on copper tube imports from both Mexico and China. Copper tube manufacturers reported to us that the rising interest in copper tube reflected the joint investigation by the Commerce Department and International Trade Commission (ITC) into whether imports of Mexican and Chinese copper tube were being sold b

elow market value in the US. In the middle of this month the Commerce Department and the ITC introduced a provisional import duty of 30% on all Mexican tube imports and a duty of between 10.26% and 60.5% on all Chinese tube imports. A final ruling on whether or not the duties will be retained is expected in September. **Restocking process may slow during Q3** According to our sources there is concern that the restocking process, which has been so instrumental in the recovery of US copper demand thus far this year, may slow during Q3. With this in mind, alongside no expected sustainable recovery in US construction activity this year, we do not expect a full recovery in US refined copper demand in 2010. Thus we forecast that US refined copper consumption will increase by 2.5% this year to ~1.6Mt. While this may seem like a healthy rate of recovery it equates to a gain of just 38kt. However, in 2011 a much stronger recovery is anticipated where demand is forecast to increase by 4.6% to just over 1.6Mt. **Negative growth forecast for US copper demand during 2010-2025** During the forecast period 2010-2025 we project that US and Canadian demand for copper will decline by 2.2% p.a. and 1.9% p.a. respectively. The negative growth will reflect structural changes in the global economy which will see manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies, such as Mexico and China. There will also be an increase in the amount of demand satisfied by imports rather than domestic production. Therefore, while the region’s wire and cable markets will be supported by the continued upgrading of North America’s electricity generation and transmission system together with the gradual upgrading of much of its other infrastructure, this will not necessarily result in increased production of North American copper wire rod. By 2025 we forecast that North American consumption will total ~1.2Mt. **Demand for copper semi products also positive** Aurubis also reported positive demand for its copper shapes during Q1 where production increased by 55% year on year to 36kt.  Similar to its wire rod output, this represented the highest level since Q2 2008.  Strong orders from the electrical and electronic and automotive sectors were largely responsible for the growth.  Another contributing factor was a stronger dollar which encouraged the exports of semi-finished products to North America and the Far East. 

**KME and Assomet report positive results** Europe’s buoyant auto sector was also responsible for both KME and Assomet reporting positive production results during Q1.  KME, who has copper semi manufacturing plants in Germany, Italy, France, UK and Spain, reported a 10.5% (+12kt) increase in its output of copper and copper alloy products in Q1 from a year earlier.  Fortunately robust orders from the auto sector and domestic appliance manufacturers helped offset weak demand from Europe’s construction sector.  According to KME several construction projects during Q1 were postponed because of bad weather in both Europe and North America.  Meanwhile in Italy, Assomet reported that the production of copper and copper alloy products increased by 19.8% year on year in Q1 to 290kt.  According to the association the output of copper semi products increased by 10%, to 150kt, during the three-month period from a year earlier while the production of copper alloy products jumped annually by 32.5% to 140kt.  In both cases this represented their highest output rate since Q2 2008.  The gain reflected healthy demand from the auto sector as well as improving orders from the manufacturers of components which are consumed by the power generation and renewable energy industries. 

**European demand expected to slow during H2** Despite the positive production results reported for Q1 there is concern that this momentum will not be maintained during H2.  There is little evidence to suggest that the recovery in orders

reflected any significant improvement in end-use demand. Our sources informed us that the pick up was largely due to restocking because of lean pipeline supplies. Therefore, once the inventory adjustment is complete demand will fall off unless there is a significant improvement in underlying demand. Indeed the latest Purchasing Managers Indices for the region suggested that the restocking boost may now be over. **Restocking boost may be over** Eurozone’s latest headline purchasing manager’s index surveys showed manufacturing activity slipping back in May from 57.5 to 56.1. More worrying was the new orders component of the index which showed a more marked decline, down from 59.6 in April to 56.9 in May. However, the greatest cause for concern was the stocks to orders ratio which slipped lower in April and May thereby suggesting that the region’s manufacturing sector completed its restocking process in Q1. Meanwhile, the eurozone PMI for the services sector (which employ’s the bulk of the region’s workforce) just crept into expansionary territory in May with a reading of 50.5. ## Japan **Strong recovery in demand for copper and copper alloy products during Q1** Demand for copper and copper alloy products recovered strongly during Q1. According to the Japan Copper and Brass Manufacturers Association, output of copper semi products increased by 120.4% from a year earlier in March. This represented the fifth consecutive month of annual increase as well as the largest annual percentage gain since the association started to collect monthly data in January 1953. The large gain partly reflected growth coming from a low base, where production in March 2009 fell by 60% from a year earlier, as well as increased export demand. The sharp gain in March meant that the production of copper and copper alloy products increased by 88.2% overall in Q1 from the corresponding period in 2009. **Demand for copper and copper alloy strip drive recovery** Demand for copper strip was particularly strong during Q1 where the Japan Copper and Brass Manufacturers Association reported a 215.5% (+45kt) annual jump in production. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - June 2010 Page 10 of 46 Copper Long-term Outlook Supporting this growth was increased export orders

which mainly reflected robust Chinese demand for digital home electronics.  Buoyant demand from Japan’s domestic semi conductor and automotive sectors also helped support the gain. **Discussions during April’s CESCO week focused on China’s growing market influence and potential smelter casualties** During CESCO Week many of our discussions with concentrate producers and consumers focused on China’s growing influence in this market as well as who, and when might there be the long-anticipated smelter casualties, given the chronic overcapacity in this sector of the market.  One conclusion was that, setting aside the relative economics of each plant, the most logical smelter closures should occur in countries that lack sufficient domestic mine feed and where refined output exceeds local demand by a considerable amount.  Countries that fit these criteria include Bulgaria, Canada, Finland, Japan, Philippines and Sweden.  That said Bulgaria should be viewed in the context of it having a wider, regional market both for concentrates feed and metals sales.  Also, developments in Canada during 2010 will see the closure of 230kt of smelting capacity by mid year (Flin Flon and Kidd Creek).  In addition, Pasar, the only smelter in the Philippines is majority owned by the world’s second largest copper concentrate trader and Boliden will soon have more domestic concentrate feed from its expanded Aitik mine and it plans to expand the electronic scrap recycling capacity at the Ronnskar plant in Sweden by 167%.  Many people that we spoke to in Santiago agreed that the next round of closures could see the loss of two smelters in Japan and one in Europe, accounting for perhaps 700kt/a of annual capacity.  As we mentioned in our previous Long Term Outlook report, the medium-term shortfall in concentrate supplies relative to the optimal global primary smelter utilisation rate (88%) is ~1.5Mt/a Cu and so the loss of three plants would amount to almost 50% of this gap.  However, there can be no guarantee that this medium-term supply gap will remain static.  We estimate that on the basis of projected smelter capacity growth and utilisation rates, China’s cathode import requirements will be around 2.6Mt/a for the next three years and this will no doubt tempt existing and potential new entrants into constructing additional smelting capacity in order to raise the levels of value-added copper production domestically.

New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles. New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it. Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply ## Scrapping rates The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration. The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years. The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years. The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. ## Scrap usage Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product. Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap. This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with

a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap.

# Principle uses of copper 

Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products.  Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use.  With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals.  This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. 

In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 33% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also he

lping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 33% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The

addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and co

pper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930 copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping.  Likewise, new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. 

Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness).  Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge.  Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added.  Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. 

Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products.  Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 8% of total copper consumption.  The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage.  The production of the new Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.

China’s government has introduced a number of measures to reduce bank lending and tighten credit conditions, which will contribute to further declines in investment through the second half of 2010, while government infrastructure projects begin to be completed. That said, the apparent soft landing in Chinese growth is what authorities have been targeting, and is an encouraging sign. We continue to expect Chinese industrial output to expand by 16.5% in 2010. There are two key developments in the Chinese economy that should be monitored closely. The first of these, which is perhaps of more immediate concern, centres on the construction industry. The possibility of a real estate bubble spurred the government to introduce a number of cooling measures this year, but authorities will be keen not to cause too severe a slowdown, as occurred in 2008, feeding through into the wider economy. The attempted solution is to limit the speculative side of the market, keeping prices in check, while forcing provincial governments to increase the supply of low-cost housing across the country. Contracts have been signed with provincial authorities that require state-owned property developers to build affordable housing, with 5.8 million new homes planned for 2010. If successful, residential construction volumes will remain robust through the year, reinforcing the strength of economic growth. If the restrictions prove to be too severe, however, the implications for wider growth could be serious. The second development concerns inflation and wages. A structural decline in the number of young workers is leading to increasing wage pressures, raising inflationary concerns. However, wage inflation is a positive development for China, as it means labour returns rising in place of corporate profits, encouraging household consumption

and shifting growth away from the capital investment model. This structural shift is a necessary one for China if it is to move towards more balanced and sustainable growth. We expect China’s economic growth to slow moderately in the next few years, but over the forecast period to 2025 to continue to grow at a robust 10.9% per year on average.
